nameStory: Whorled Coreopsis gets its name from its leaves that grow in circles around the stem at each joint, creating distinct "whorls" - like spokes on a wheel. The "Coreopsis" part comes from Greek words meaning "bug-like," referring to how the seeds look like tiny ticks or beetles. That's why plants in this group are also called "tickseeds" - their dark, oval seeds really do look like little bugs clinging to the flower heads!
description: Whorled Coreopsis is a cheerful perennial wildflower that looks like a miniature sunflower garden. It grows 1-3 feet tall and spreads into neat clumps covered with bright yellow, daisy-like flowers from summer into fall. The plant gets its name from its distinctive thread-like leaves that circle around the stem in whorls, giving it a delicate, almost feathery appearance. This native wildflower is sometimes called "pot-of-gold" for its abundant golden blooms.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thread-thin leaves arranged in distinct circles (whorls) around the stem at each joint, feeling soft and almost needle-like to the touch but not sharp or prickly

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow daisy-like flowers about 1-2 inches across with 8 notched petals that feel papery when rubbed between fingers, and a darker yellow center

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms tidy, bushy clumps that spread slowly by underground stems, with multiple upright stems that feel sturdy but bend easily

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark, oval seeds that really do look like tiny ticks or beetles clinging to the spent flower heads - this is where the "tickseed" name comes from

habitat: In New England, Whorled Coreopsis is most commonly found as an escaped garden plant in disturbed areas, roadsides, and field edges, though it occasionally appears in open woodlands and meadows. It thrives in well-drained soils and full to partial sun, often growing alongside other naturalized wildflowers like Black-eyed Susan and Wild Bergamot.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small tufts of thread-like leaves in distinctive whorled arrangements around reddish stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with masses of bright yellow flowers that attract butterflies and bees, continuing to produce new blooms through hot weather.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, then develop into seed heads full of dark, tick-like seeds that birds enjoy eating.
seasonality.winter: Stems die back to ground level, leaving only the underground portions alive to regrow next spring.

funFact: This plant is so tough that it's often used in "drought-proof" gardens because its thread-like leaves have a secret superpower - they lose very little water compared to broad leaves, letting the plant bloom cheerfully through summer heat waves that wilt other flowers!
confusionNotes: The thread-like leaves in perfect whorls make this almost impossible to confuse with other plants - most people mistake it for some kind of herb or unusual grass until they see the bright yellow flowers. If you see yellow daisy-like flowers on a plant with needle-thin leaves arranged in circles, you've found Whorled Coreopsis!
contextualKnowledge: While native to the southeastern United States, Whorled Coreopsis has become widely planted and naturalized in New England gardens because of its long blooming period and drought tolerance. Don't worry if you find it "wild" - it's not invasive and plays nicely with native plants.
compareHints: Among its tickseed relatives, Whorled Coreopsis is the only one with thread-like leaves arranged in distinct whorls around the stem. Rose Coreopsis has broader leaves and pink flowers, while Lance-leaved Coreopsis has much wider, spear-shaped leaves. The whorled leaf arrangement is unique among all the Coreopsis species you'll find in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rose Coreopsis is the only tickseed in New England with pink or white petals - all its relatives like Lance-leaved and Whorled Coreopsis have bright yellow flowers.

Lance-leaved Coreopsis differs from other Coreopsis species by its simple, unlobed lance-shaped leaves - Rose Coreopsis has much smaller pink flowers, while Whorled Coreopsis has very finely divided, thread-like leaves.
Plains coreopsis differs from other New England coreopsis species by being an annual (dies each year) rather than perennial, and by having the most deeply divided, feathery leaves of the group.
Tall coreopsis dwarfs all other New England coreopsis species - most relatives like lance-leaved coreopsis and rose coreopsis stay under 3 feet tall.

Among New England's coreopsis species, lobed coreopsis is immediately distinguished by its uniquely shaped leaves - rose coreopsis has narrow linear leaves, lance-leaved has simple spear-shaped leaves, and whorled coreopsis has thread-like leaves in circles around the stem.

Large-flowered tickseed stands out from other New England tickseeds by its size - both the flowers and overall plant are notably larger than rose coreopsis (which has pink flowers) or lance-leaved coreopsis.

Unlike its New England relatives like Lance-leaved Coreopsis (which has simple, narrow leaves) or Rose Coreopsis (which has thin, needle-like leaves), Prairie Coreopsis has those distinctive deeply-divided, finger-like leaves that make it unmistakable.
